rows.verified: Compressed air can cause serious injury through bodily entry, skin penetration and high-velocity particles.
Compressed-air systems can create explosion and overpressurisation hazards.
Blockages, control failure, overspeed, external fire, overheating and deposits can contribute to dangerous pressure conditions.
Safety management should cover compressors, receivers, dryers, coolers, distribution lines, actuators and pneumatic equipment.
Inspection, maintenance, competent installation, safe use and worker training are core compressed-air controls.
Compressed-air construction work requires safe systems, competent people, suitable plant and controlled compression and decompression procedures.
The regulatory framework includes health surveillance, medical support, emergency arrangements, fire precautions and exposure records.
Working in compressed air can cause decompression sickness, barotrauma and dysbaric osteonecrosis.
Compressed-air risk depends on pressure, system design, equipment condition, task, exposure profile, decompression procedure and competence.
Compressed-air evidence is system-, task-, pressure-, worker- and condition-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury probability.
Frequent or prolonged wet work can irritate skin and contribute to occupational dermatitis.
Ingredients in cleaning products can cause skin allergy or occupational asthma.
Corrosive cleaning products can cause skin burns and serious eye injury.
Good work techniques should minimise direct contact, leaks and spills, with cleaning chemicals stored safely.
Appropriate gloves, aprons and eye protection may be required where exposure cannot otherwise be adequately controlled.
Prompt decontamination, thorough drying, skin care and effective ventilation help reduce exposure and skin damage.
Catering fumes can contain oil mist, smoke, irritants and carbon monoxide from fuel-burning equipment.
Extractor hoods or canopies can be required above cooking appliances to capture fumes at source.
Cleaning and catering risk depends on product chemistry, dilution, incompatibilities, task, contact time, ventilation, hygiene and PPE selection.
Cleaning and catering evidence is chemical-, task-, worker-, ventilation- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level illness probability.
